blocks.text: A birth injury is physical harm a baby suffers before, during, or shortly after delivery. Unlike a birth defect (which develops from genetics or events during pregnancy that no one caused), some birth injuries are caused by medical negligence — and the law gives your family the right to seek justice and lifetime resources.
Movement & muscle-tone disorders from birth asphyxia.

Brain damage from untreated newborn jaundice.

Delayed care during a maternal & fetal emergency.

Missed or delayed bilirubin screening and follow-up.

blocks.text: A cerebral palsy diagnosis is life-changing. If it followed a difficult delivery, it's worth finding out whether negligence played a role — and what that could mean for your family's future.
Medically reviewed · By [MEDICAL REVIEWER], [CREDENTIALS] · Sources: CDC, AAP · Legally reviewed by Larry F. Taylor, Jr.

Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of disorders affecting movement, muscle tone and posture, caused by damage to the developing brain — most often around the time of birth. Severity ranges from mild coordination issues to significant physical and cognitive disability.

CP is commonly linked to oxygen deprivation (birth asphyxia) during labor and delivery, premature birth, infections, or trauma. According to the CDC, some cases are directly tied to how labor complications were managed.

items: Delayed milestones (rolling over, sitting, walking)
Stiff or floppy muscle tone
Unusual posture or favoring one side of the body
Difficulty with fine motor skills or feeding

blocks.text: Pediatricians typically diagnose CP through developmental monitoring, neurological exams and imaging (MRI or CT), often by age 2, per AAP guidance.
There is no cure, but physical, occupational and speech therapy, medication, orthopedic care and adaptive equipment can significantly improve quality of life — often at substantial lifetime cost.

When medical teams fail to monitor fetal distress, delay an emergency C-section, or misuse delivery instruments, the brain can be deprived of oxygen long enough to cause permanent damage. These are the moments our investigations focus on.

If negligence during labor and delivery contributed to your child's cerebral palsy, your family may be entitled to compensation for lifetime care. Deadlines to file vary by state — see your state's page for details.
Cerebral palsy cases can involve lifetime therapy, equipment, home modifications, lost future income and pain and suffering. A free case review helps estimate what your family's claim may be worth.

Attorney Larry F. Taylor, Jr. works with medical experts and life-care planners to prove what went wrong and what care will cost over a lifetime. Larry is based in Texas and licensed across Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico and Arizona, and partners with trusted co-counsel and associates nationwide.

blocks.text: Kernicterus is almost entirely preventable with proper newborn jaundice screening and treatment. When it happens, it's worth understanding why.
Medically reviewed · By [MEDICAL REVIEWER], [CREDENTIALS] · Sources: AAP, NIH · Legally reviewed by Larry F. Taylor, Jr.
Kernicterus is a rare but severe type of brain damage caused by very high, untreated levels of bilirubin in a newborn's blood — a condition known as hyperbilirubinemia, or newborn jaundice.
Nearly all newborns have some jaundice as their liver matures. It becomes dangerous when bilirubin levels rise unchecked — most often because screening or follow-up care was missed or delayed.

items: Yellowing of the skin and eyes that worsens after day 3-4
Extreme sleepiness or difficulty feeding
High-pitched crying or arching of the back
Poor muscle tone

blocks.text: Standard care per AAP guidelines includes bilirubin screening before hospital discharge and a follow-up visit within days — the screening step most often missed in kernicterus cases.
Caught early, jaundice is treated simply with phototherapy. Once kernicterus sets in, resulting damage — often affecting hearing, movement and vision — is permanent.

Kernicterus is considered a 'never event' in much of the medical community — it should not happen when screening protocols are followed. Missed bilirubin checks, ignored parent concerns, or premature discharge are common failure points.
Because kernicterus is largely preventable, these cases often present clear evidence of a missed standard of care. A free case review can help you understand your options.
Claims may account for lifetime medical & hearing/vision support, special education needs, and pain and suffering.

American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) clinical practice guideline on hyperbilirubinemia. National Institutes of Health (NIH). This page is for general information only and is not medical or legal advice.

items.q: Is kernicterus common?
items.a: It's rare today precisely because screening protocols work well when followed — which is why most cases involve a missed step in care.

items.q: Can jaundice be treated at home?
items.a: Mild jaundice often resolves on its own, but severe or rapidly rising levels require prompt medical treatment — always follow your pediatrician's guidance.

items.q: What if my baby was discharged without a bilirubin check?
items.a: That may be relevant to a negligence claim. A free case review can help you understand what happened.

blocks.text: When a baby's shoulder gets stuck during delivery, how the medical team responds in those seconds can determine whether a nerve injury like Erb's palsy is permanent.
Medically reviewed · By [MEDICAL REVIEWER], [CREDENTIALS] · Sources: ACOG · Legally reviewed by Larry F. Taylor, Jr.

Shoulder dystocia occurs when a baby's shoulder becomes lodged behind the mother's pelvic bone during delivery. If handled improperly, the resulting stretching or tearing of the brachial plexus nerves can cause Erb's palsy or other nerve damage in the baby's arm.
Risk factors include large babies, maternal diabetes, and prolonged labor — but injury most often results from excessive pulling or improper maneuvers used to free the shoulder.

items: Limp or weak arm on one side (Erb's palsy)
Lack of movement or grip in the affected hand
Arm held in a bent, rotated position

blocks.text: Diagnosed through physical exam and imaging shortly after birth, with severity assessed over the following weeks as nerves either recover or show permanent damage.
Physical therapy helps many infants regain function; severe cases may require nerve grafting or reconstructive surgery, sometimes with lifelong limitations.

ACOG-recommended maneuvers exist to manage shoulder dystocia safely. Excessive downward traction on the head, rather than following those protocols, is a leading cause of preventable brachial plexus injury.
If your child's arm injury followed a difficult delivery, a records review can clarify whether recommended delivery maneuvers were followed.
Claims may cover ongoing physical therapy, potential surgery, adaptive needs and long-term impact on earning capacity.
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) practice guidance on shoulder dystocia management. This page is for general information only and is not medical or legal advice.

items.q: Does Erb's palsy always resolve?
items.a: Many infants recover significant function with therapy, but moderate to severe cases can result in permanent limitation.

items.q: How soon should I seek legal advice?
items.a: As soon as possible — medical records and delivery notes are most complete and available early.

blocks.text: Placental abruption is a true obstetric emergency for mother and baby. When warning signs are missed or care is delayed, the consequences can be severe.
Medically reviewed · By [MEDICAL REVIEWER], [CREDENTIALS] · Sources: ACOG, NIH · Legally reviewed by Larry F. Taylor, Jr.
Placental abruption happens when the placenta partially or fully separates from the uterine wall before delivery, cutting off oxygen and nutrients to the baby and causing heavy maternal bleeding.
Risk factors include high blood pressure, trauma, and prior abruption — but regardless of cause, it requires immediate recognition and action once symptoms appear.

items: Sudden vaginal bleeding
Severe abdominal or back pain
Uterine tenderness or rigidity
Decreased fetal movement

blocks.text: Diagnosed via physical exam, ultrasound and continuous fetal monitoring — speed matters, since severity can escalate quickly.
Depending on severity, treatment ranges from monitoring to emergency delivery — often by C-section — to protect mother and baby.
Delayed recognition of bleeding or fetal distress, failure to order an emergency delivery, or dismissing a mother's reported symptoms can turn a manageable emergency into a preventable tragedy.
If care was delayed after abruption symptoms appeared, that delay — and its consequences for mother or baby — deserves review.
Claims may address injuries to mother and baby, ongoing medical needs, and pain and suffering.
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG). National Institutes of Health (NIH). This page is for general information only and is not medical or legal advice.

items.q: Is placental abruption always an emergency?
items.a: Yes — any suspected abruption requires immediate evaluation, since both maternal and fetal outcomes depend on how quickly it is addressed.

items.q: Can placental abruption cause HIE?
items.a: Yes, prolonged oxygen deprivation from abruption can lead to hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy in the baby.

items.q: Do I have a car accident case?
items.a: If you were injured or suffered losses in a crash that wasn't entirely your fault, you likely have a claim. A free case review can confirm exactly where you stand.

items.q: What should I do immediately after a car accident?
items.a: Get medical attention, call the police, document the scene with photos, exchange information, and avoid giving a recorded statement to any insurance company before speaking with a lawyer.

items.q: How long do I have to file a claim?
items.a: It varies by state — generally two years in Texas, Oklahoma and Arizona, and three years in New Mexico. Deadlines can be shorter in some situations, so contact us promptly.

items.q: What if I was partly at fault for the accident?
items.a: You may still recover compensation. Texas and Oklahoma reduce your recovery by your percentage of fault and bar it entirely past 51%; New Mexico and Arizona use pure comparative fault, so you can recover even if you were mostly at fault, reduced by your share.

items.q: What if the other driver was uninsured or underinsured?

items.q: I was hurt in a rideshare (Uber or Lyft) accident — is it different?
items.a: Yes — rideshare companies carry large commercial policies, but coverage often depends on exactly what stage of the ride the driver was in when the crash happened. We sort out which policy applies.

items.q: What if it was a hit-and-run?
items.a: Hit-and-run cases often rely on your own uninsured motorist coverage and any evidence — dashcam, witnesses, traffic cameras — that can help identify the other driver.

blocks.text: Mass Tort Lawyer — Dangerous Drugs, Devices & Toxic Exposure

A mass tort is a legal action where many people are harmed by the same product or conduct — often a defective drug, medical device, or toxic exposure. Unlike a class action, each person keeps an individual claim, frequently coordinated in federal court as multidistrict litigation (MDL).
Medications that caused harm through undisclosed risks or manufacturing defects.
Implants and devices — hernia mesh, hip implants, IVC filters and more — that failed or caused injury.
Environmental and workplace exposure to contaminated water, chemicals, or harmful products.

blocks.title: You file your own individual claim
blocks.text: A mass tort keeps your case separate — your compensation depends on your own injuries and damages, not a shared class-wide pool.

blocks.title: Cases are coordinated, not combined
blocks.text: Similar claims are often coordinated in federal court as multidistrict litigation (MDL) for efficiency, while each case stays individually yours.

blocks.title: Bellwether trials or settlement
blocks.text: Early 'bellwether' trials or negotiated settlement programs often shape how remaining cases, including yours, are resolved.
Do I have a mass tort claim?
If you were harmed by a product named in active litigation, you may qualify — even if you live in a different state.

items.q: Is a mass tort the same as a class action?
items.a: No — in a mass tort you keep your own individual claim and potential recovery, unlike a single class-wide judgment.

items.q: What does it cost?
items.a: Nothing up front — mass torts are handled on contingency.

items.q: What is an MDL?
items.a: Multidistrict litigation coordinates similar federal cases before one judge for efficiency — it speeds up the process without merging your individual claim into anyone else's.

items.q: Can I qualify if I live outside Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico or Arizona?
items.a: Often, yes — mass torts frequently involve claimants nationwide.

items.q: Who can file a wrongful death claim?
items.a: It varies by state — often a spouse, children, or parents, or a personal representative of the estate. We'll confirm for your situation.

items.q: How long do we have?
items.a: Deadlines vary by state, often two to three years. Please contact us promptly so we can confirm your timeline.

items.q: Is this different from a criminal case?
items.a: Yes — a wrongful death claim is separate from any criminal case, and can proceed regardless of whether criminal charges are filed.

items.q: What does it cost to speak with you?
items.a: Nothing. Consultations are free and confidential, and we work on contingency — no fee unless we recover for your family.

blocks.text: A misdiagnosis is malpractice when a competent provider would have reached the correct diagnosis and the error caused harm — for example, a missed or delayed cancer, heart attack, stroke, or infection diagnosis that worsened the outcome.

items: Cancer (breast, lung, colon)
Heart attack / stroke
Infections & sepsis
Failure to order or act on tests

blocks.text: We work with specialist physicians to show what a reasonable provider would have found and how the delay changed your prognosis.

items.q: Is every wrong diagnosis malpractice?
items.a: No — only when the error falls below the standard of care and caused harm.

blocks.text: Surgical errors are preventable mistakes that fall below the standard of care — wrong-site or wrong-patient surgery, retained instruments/sponges, anesthesia errors, or avoidable nerve/organ damage.
Some surgical errors are so serious they're called 'never events' — they should never happen with proper care.
We obtain the operative and anesthesia records and work with surgical experts to prove the breach and its harm.
When a prescription or over-the-counter drug causes serious harm — due to inadequate warnings, contamination, or a defect — injured people can pursue the manufacturer, often through a mass tort/MDL.
You may qualify if you took the drug and suffered a linked injury within the relevant time frame.

When an implant or device (e.g., hernia mesh, hip implants, IVC filters, CPAP machines) is defectively designed, manufactured, or inadequately warned about and causes harm, victims can pursue the maker — often via a mass tort/MDL.
You may qualify if you received the device and suffered a linked complication.
When people are harmed by exposure to a harmful substance (e.g., contaminated water, industrial chemicals, certain consumer products), they may pursue those responsible — often as a mass tort.
You may qualify if you were exposed and developed a linked illness.

Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) is brain injury caused by oxygen deprivation around the time of birth. Timely recognition and treatment — including therapeutic hypothermia (cooling) — can reduce the harm.
Medically reviewed · By [MEDICAL REVIEWER], [CREDENTIALS] · Sources: NIH/NINDS, ACOG/AAP · Legally reviewed by Larry F. Taylor, Jr.

Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) is brain injury caused by a lack of oxygen and blood flow to a baby's brain around the time of birth. It frequently leads to cerebral palsy and other lifelong conditions.
HIE is often preventable with proper fetal monitoring and a timely response to signs of distress. When negligence caused the oxygen deprivation, families may have a claim.

items: Failure to monitor the fetal heart rate
Delay in delivering a baby in distress
Failure to recognize or treat cord or placental problems
Failure to offer timely cooling therapy

blocks.text: Therapeutic hypothermia (cooling) lowers a newborn's body temperature in the hours after birth to limit brain injury — a delay in offering it, when indicated, can be negligence.

HIE can require lifelong care and therapy. A successful claim can fund lifetime medical care, therapy, equipment, special education, home and vehicle modifications, lost earning capacity, and pain and suffering.

National Institutes of Health (NIH) / NINDS. American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) and American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) neonatal encephalopathy guidance. This page is for general information only and is not medical or legal advice.

items.q: Is HIE the same as cerebral palsy?
items.a: No — HIE is the oxygen-related brain injury; it can lead to cerebral palsy and other conditions.

items.q: What is cooling therapy?
items.a: Therapeutic hypothermia lowers the newborn's body temperature to limit brain injury; delay in offering it can be negligence.
